h1: Pitching a brewery to angel investors and the numbers they check
title: Pitching a Brewery to Angel Investors | Craft Beer School
desc: The numbers angel investors check in an Indian brewery pitch: capex, licence status, unit economics, ramp-up, cash runway and how they get their money back.
teaser: Investors love a good beer story. Then they open the spreadsheet and ask how long the money lasts.
standfirst: An angel investor can like your beer and still say no. What decides it is usually a handful of numbers and how confidently you explain them. Here is what they check and how to prepare.
sections: Angels invest in the founder and the model

Angel investors put their own money into early businesses. For a brewery they are betting on three things: that you can build and run it, that the numbers can work and that they will one day see a return. The story of why you love beer gets you the meeting. It does not get you the cheque.

Breweries are an unusual pitch for many Indian angels, who see far more software and consumer start-ups. Capital is heavy, licences are slow, excise rules vary by state and growth is physical rather than viral. Expect them to probe exactly those points.

Most serious investors will ask where you stand on licences before they look at the beer. A brewery without its excise licence is a plan, not a business. Delays are common. Show where each permission stands: land use and building approvals, pollution control consent, fire safety, FSSAI, excise and any local trade licences. Our brewery compliance checklist is a useful framework. Be honest about what is pending and how long it might take.

Investors want to see the full capital cost, not just the brewhouse quote. Break it down: brewhouse and tanks, chiller and cold room, utilities, building work and fit-out, kitchen if any, licences and deposits, pre-opening salaries and a contingency. Show which quotes are firm and which are estimates. A contingency line of zero tells an investor you have not done this before.

Then show working capital separately: raw materials, excise paid in advance where that applies, the gap between paying suppliers and receiving payment. Many brewery plans fail because the money runs out after the building is finished but before sales settle.

Investors will want the cost and margin of a single unit: a litre, a pint or a case. That means:

  • Raw material cost per litre, from your recipe and expected brewhouse yield.
  • Excise and taxes per litre, according to your state's structure.
  • Packaging cost per unit, if you package.
  • Selling price per unit by channel, with the margin left after each step.

Our guide to cost per litre of beer shows how to build that number. If you cannot explain your gross margin per pint in one sentence, practise until you can.

No brewpub is full in month one. Show a realistic ramp-up of sales over the first year or two, a month when the business covers its costs and how much cash you hold until then. Investors look closely at runway: how many months the business can survive if sales are slower than planned. Show a downside case with sales thirty percent below plan and explain what you would cut. That one slide often builds more trust than a beautiful forecast.

Market claims need care. Talk about real demand you can show, such as trial batches, pre-bookings or a following. Avoid unsourced market size numbers. Investors have heard them all.
How they get their money back

Angels want to understand the return. Is it a share of profits, a later buyback, a sale of the business or growth into multiple outlets that attracts larger investors? Be clear on how much you are raising, what it buys, the equity you are offering and what milestones the money reaches. Our guide to brewery funding options explains the alternatives to angel money.

Use a lawyer and a chartered accountant for valuation, shareholder agreements and compliance. Raising money from investors in India has its own legal process. Getting it wrong creates problems later.

Investors back people. Show who does what: who brews, who runs the floor, who handles finance and compliance. If the head brewer is not yet hired, say how and when you will hire them and what the role will pay in the plan. Our guide to the brewery business plan covers how to present the team alongside the numbers.

Gaps are normal at this stage. Hiding them is not. An investor who discovers after the cheque that nobody on the team has run a commercial kitchen will lose trust quickly.
Prepare for the questions you dread

Write down the five questions you hope nobody asks. Licence delay. Head brewer leaves. Rent rises. A state changes its excise policy. A competitor opens across the road. Prepare a clear answer for each. Investors do not expect you to have removed every risk. They expect you to have seen them.
faqs: What do angel investors look for in a brewery?
A capable team, a clear licence position, realistic capex and working capital, sound unit economics and a believable path to a return.
Should I pitch before getting my brewery licence?
You can, but investors will treat the licence as the biggest risk. Show exactly where each permission stands and the realistic timeline.
Do I need a lawyer for an angel round?
Yes. Shareholder agreements, valuations and investor compliance have legal consequences, so use a lawyer and a chartered accountant.
